claim: The resting primate brain is traversed by spontaneous functional connectivity patterns that show striking differences between conscious and unconscious states.
source: The resting primate brain is traversed by spontaneous functional connectivity patterns that show striking differences between conscious and unconscious states.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction and by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) can improve signs of consciousness in disorders of consciousness (DOCs).
source: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a non-invasive neuromodulatory technique, can improve signs of consciousness in disorders of consciousness (DOCs)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies in the introduction section.

claim: In awake macaques receiving either anodal or cathodal tDCS, cathodal stimulation robustly disrupted the repertoire of functional connectivity patterns.
source: In awake macaques receiving either anodal or cathodal tDCS, we found that cathodal stimulation robustly disrupted the repertoire of functional connectivity patterns
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 5 and statistical analyses in Table 4.

claim: Cathodal tDCS increased structure–function correlation (SFC) in awake macaques.
source: In awake macaques receiving either anodal or cathodal tDCS, we found that cathodal stimulation robustly disrupted the repertoire of functional connectivity patterns, increased structure–function correlation (SFC)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F, G and statistical analyses in Table 4.

claim: Cathodal tDCS decreased Shannon entropy in awake macaques.
source: In awake macaques receiving either anodal or cathodal tDCS, we found that cathodal stimulation robustly disrupted the repertoire of functional connectivity patterns, increased structure–function correlation (SFC), decreased Shannon entropy
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and statistical analyses in Table 4.

claim: Cathodal tDCS favored transitions toward anatomically based patterns in awake macaques.
source: In awake macaques receiving either anodal or cathodal tDCS, we found that cathodal stimulation robustly disrupted the repertoire of functional connectivity patterns, increased structure–function correlation (SFC), decreased Shannon entropy, and favored transitions toward anatomically based patterns.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and statistical analyses in Table 5.

claim: Under deep sedation, anodal tDCS significantly altered brain pattern distribution.
source: Under deep sedation, anodal tDCS significantly altered brain pattern distribution and reduced SFC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7 and statistical analyses in Table 7.

claim: Under deep sedation, anodal tDCS reduced structure-function correlation (SFC).
source: Under deep sedation, anodal tDCS significantly altered brain pattern distribution and reduced SFC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7 and statistical analyses in Table 7.

claim: Prefrontal stimulation modified dynamic connectivity arrangements typically associated with consciousness and unconsciousness.
source: The prefrontal stimulation also modified dynamic connectivity arrangements typically associated with consciousness and unconsciousness.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing awake and anesthetized states shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: PFC tDCS induces striking modifications in the fMRI-based dynamic organization of the brain across different states of consciousness.
source: Our findings offer compelling evidence that PFC tDCS induces striking modifications in the fMRI-based dynamic organization of the brain across different states of consciousness.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At rest, the spontaneous activity of the awake brain is highly structured.
source: At rest, the spontaneous activity of the awake brain is highly structured.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: The brain dynamically transitions through various resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) patterns, which are thought to support specific cognitive functions.
source: The brain dynamically transitions through various resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) patterns, which are thought to support specific cognitive functions (Deco et al., 2013; Fox et al., 2006; Vincent et al., 2006; Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Raichle et al., 2001; Calhoun et al., 2014; Preti et al., 2017; Baker et al., 2014; Deco et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In non-human primates (NHPs), the induction of wakefulness and unconsciousness by different anesthetics is associated with strikingly different sequences and occurrences of transient brain patterns.
source: Interestingly, in non-human primates (NHPs), the induction of wakefulness and unconsciousness by different anesthetics is associated with strikingly different sequences and occurrences of transient brain patterns (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Uhrig et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The conscious brain is traversed by a diverse and mobile set of functional brain patterns that deviate from anatomical connectivity.
source: The conscious brain is traversed by a diverse and mobile set of functional brain patterns that deviate from anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The unconscious brain is characterized by transient functional patterns that are less diverse, stiffer, and more closely follow anatomical connectivity.
source: In contrast, the unconscious brain is characterized by transient functional patterns that are less diverse, stiffer, and more closely follow anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar dynamic functional configurations are found in awake and sedated humans and generalize to other contexts of loss of consciousness, whether in patients with impaired consciousness or during sleep.
source: Similar dynamic functional configurations are found in awake and sedated humans and generalize to other contexts of loss of consciousness, whether in patients with impaired consciousness or during sleep (Luppi et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2020; Demertzi et al., 2019; Golkowski et al., 2019; Castro et al., 2024b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Different structure–function configurations are proposed as signatures of consciousness and unconsciousness.
source: Ultimately, these different structure–function configurations are proposed as signatures of consciousness and unconsciousness, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: tDCS acts through diverse, concurrent, and multiscale modes of action.
source: In vivo and in vitro data suggest that tDCS acts through diverse, concurrent, and multiscale modes of action (Lefaucheur et al., 2017; Lefaucheur and Wendling, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ongoing neural activity during tDCS administration is likely to be critical, as tDCS effects are state-dependent and primarily modulate active networks.
source: Importantly, ongoing neural activity during tDCS administration is likely to be critical, as tDCS effects are state-dependent and primarily modulate active networks (Antal et al., 2007; Bikson et al., 2013; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Anodal tDCS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) improves signs of consciousness in patients with disorders of consciousness (DOCs).
source: Anodal tDCS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) improves signs of consciousness in patients with disorders of consciousness (DOCs) (Thibaut et al., 2014; Angelakis et al., 2014; Hermann et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to clinical studies.

claim: Anodal tDCS of the left DLPFC can increase rs-fMRI connectivity in some DOC patients, both at the site of stimulation and in remote regions.
source: Anodal tDCS of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) improves signs of consciousness in patients with disorders of consciousness (DOCs) (Thibaut et al., 2014; Angelakis et al., 2014; Hermann et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023) and can increase rs-fMRI connectivity in some of these patients, both at the site of stimulation and in remote regions (Peng et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The effects of prefrontal cortex (PFC) tDCS on resting-state dynamic brain patterns which are typically associated with consciousness have never been investigated.
source: However, the effects of prefrontal cortex (PFC) tDCS on resting-state dynamic brain patterns which are typically associated with consciousness have never been investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study.

claim: In healthy humans, tDCS can perturb both occurrences and transitions of some rs-fMRI co-activation patterns (CAPs).
source: In healthy humans, tDCS can perturb both occurrences and transitions of some rs-fMRI co-activation patterns (CAPs) (using the DLPFC as a seed), suggesting that some elements of brain dynamics could be affected by tDCS in the awake resting brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from prior research.

claim: Repeated stimulation of the rat motor cortex facilitates the return of the righting reflex and visual and working memory after isoflurane anesthesia.
source: Repeated stimulation of the rat motor cortex facilitates the return of the righting reflex and visual and working memory after isoflurane anesthesia (Mansouri and García, 2021), suggesting that tDCS may represent a novel approach to accelerate recovery from general anesthesia (Kato and Solt, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: tDCS may represent a novel approach to accelerate recovery from general anesthesia.
source: Repeated stimulation of the rat motor cortex facilitates the return of the righting reflex and visual and working memory after isoflurane anesthesia (Mansouri and García, 2021), suggesting that tDCS may represent a novel approach to accelerate recovery from general anesthesia (Kato and Solt, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from prior research.

claim: Anodal prefrontal tDCS had only a marginal effect on brain dynamics in awake animals.
source: Our results provide evidence that anodal prefrontal tDCS had only a marginal effect on brain dynamics in awake animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Cathodal prefrontal tDCS significantly reorganized the functional repertoire in favor of anatomically similar brain patterns without apparent behavioral modification in awake animals.
source: In contrast, cathodal prefrontal tDCS significantly reorganized the functional repertoire in favor of anatomically similar brain patterns without apparent behavioral modification.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5 and behavioral data in Table 2.

claim: Both anodal and cathodal stimulation affected the Markov chain transitions between brain patterns, with some changes specific to ongoing stimulation and others to the post-stimulation period.
source: Moreover, both anodal and cathodal stimulation affected the Markov chain transitions between brain patterns, with some changes specific to ongoing stimulation and others to the post-stimulation period.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and statistical analyses in Table 5.

claim: Under anesthesia, anodal prefrontal tDCS delivered at an intensity of 2 mA, but not 1 mA, significantly reduced the SFC.
source: Under anesthesia, anodal prefrontal tDCS delivered at an intensity of 2 mA, but not 1 mA, significantly reduced the SFC
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7 and statistical analyses in Table 7.

claim: Anodal prefrontal tDCS at 2 mA did not fully restore the broad and rich dynamic repertoire of functional patterns characteristic of wakefulness under anesthesia.
source: Under anesthesia, anodal prefrontal tDCS delivered at an intensity of 2 mA, but not 1 mA, significantly reduced the SFC but did not fully restore the broad and rich dynamic repertoire of functional patterns characteristic of wakefulness
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Anodal prefrontal tDCS at 2 mA did not induce signs of arousal in anesthetized animals.
source: Under anesthesia, anodal prefrontal tDCS delivered at an intensity of 2 mA, but not 1 mA, significantly reduced the SFC but did not fully restore the broad and rich dynamic repertoire of functional patterns characteristic of wakefulness, nor did it induce signs of arousal in the animals.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations during the experiments.

claim: tDCS modulates conscious and unconscious brain dynamics in a polarity- and intensity-dependent manner.
source: Altogether, these findings illustrate the ability of tDCS to modulate conscious and unconscious brain dynamics in a polarity- and intensity-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Four rhesus monkeys (M. mulatta, 18–20 years, 7.2–9.8 kg) were scanned.
source: Four rhesus monkeys (M. mulatta, 18–20 years, 7.2–9.8 kg) were scanned.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

source: Two males were tested for the awake experiments (monkeys J and Y)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: One female and one male were tested for experiments under anesthesia (monkeys R and N).
source: one female and one male were tested for experiments under anesthesia (monkeys R and N).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The sample size is comparable to previous work in NHP using fMRI.
source: Our sample size is comparable to previous work in NHP using fMRI (Milham et al., 2018; Yacoub et al., 2020; Uchimura et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All procedures followed the European Convention for Animal Care (86-406) and the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
source: All procedures followed the European Convention for Animal Care (86-406) and the National Institutes of Health's Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

source: Animal studies were approved by the Institutional Ethical Committee (CETEA protocol #16-040).

source: We applied tDCS using a battery-powered stimulator (1 × 1 tES device, Soterix medical) located outside the scanner room
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

source: We used a 1 × 1 electrode montage with two carbon rubber electrodes (dimensions: 1.4 cm × 1.85 cm, 0.93 cm thick) inserted into Soterix HD-tES MRI electrode holders (base diameter: 25 mm; height: 10.5 mm), which are in contact with the scalp.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The electrodes used (2.59 cm2) are smaller than conventional tDCS sponge electrodes (typically 25–35 cm2).
source: These electrodes (2.59 cm2) are smaller than conventional tDCS sponge electrodes (typically 25–35 cm2).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Electrode contact quality was checked before all stimulation sessions using the device's Pre-stim Tickle function (1 mA for 30 s).
source: Electrode contact quality was checked before all stimulation sessions using the device's Pre-stim Tickle function (1 mA for 30 s).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The current was gradually increased from 0 mA to the target intensity over the first 30 s to reduce the likelihood of the monkeys experiencing discomfort at the electrode sites.
source: To reduce the likelihood of the monkeys experiencing discomfort at the electrode sites, the current was gradually increased from 0 mA to the target intensity over the first 30 s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The current was gradually decreased to 0 mA over the last 30 s of each tDCS stimulation period.
source: The current was also gradually decreased to 0 mA over the last 30 s of each tDCS stimulation period.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

source: The tDCS device was turned off during the acquisition of the pre- and post-stimulation fMRI blocks to avoid any hypothetical biological effect of the residual current (Fonteneau et al., 2019), which we measured to be 0.023 mA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The residual current was measured to be 0.023 mA.
source: The tDCS device was turned off during the acquisition of the pre- and post-stimulation fMRI blocks to avoid any hypothetical biological effect of the residual current (Fonteneau et al., 2019), which we measured to be 0.023 mA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: None of the monkeys showed any side effects after the tDCS-fMRI scanning sessions.
source: After the tDCS-fMRI scanning sessions, the monkeys' scalps were examined for redness, skin burns, or other lesions. None of the monkeys showed any side effects.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental results.

claim: In the awake experiments, tDCS was delivered for 20 min at a current intensity of 2 mA.
source: tDCS was delivered for 20 min at a current intensity of 2 mA.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: For anesthesia experiments, two 20-min blocks of anodal tDCS stimulation were applied consecutively in each scanning session, with a current intensity of 1 mA for the first block and 2 mA for the second block.
source: Two 20-min blocks of anodal tDCS stimulation were applied consecutively in each scanning session, with a current intensity of 1 mA for the first block and 2 mA for the second block (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The monkeys were scanned on a 3-T horizontal scanner (Siemens Prisma Fit, Erlanger, Germany) with a custom-built single transmit-receiver surface coil.
source: The monkeys were scanned on a 3-T horizontal scanner (Siemens Prisma Fit, Erlanger, Germany) with a custom-built single transmit-receiver surface coil.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Before each scanning session, monocrystalline iron oxide nanoparticles (10 mg/kg, i.v.; MION, Feraheme, AMAG Pharmaceuticals, MA) were injected into the saphenous vein of the monkey to improve the contrast-to-noise ratio and the spatial selectivity of the MR signal changes.
source: Before each scanning session, monocrystalline iron oxide nanoparticles (10 mg/kg, i.v.; MION, Feraheme, AMAG Pharmaceuticals, MA) were injected into the saphenous vein of the monkey to improve the contrast-to-noise ratio and the spatial selectivity of the MR signal changes (Vanduffel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: All fMRI data were acquired while the monkeys were engaged in a passive event-related auditory task, the local–global paradigm.
source: All fMRI data were acquired while the monkeys were engaged in a passive event-related auditory task, the local–global paradigm, which is based on local and global deviations from temporal regularities (Bekinschtein et al., 2009; Uhrig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A total of 288 runs were acquired in the awake state.
source: A total of 288 runs were acquired in the awake state: 136 runs before stimulation, 56 runs during anodal stimulation, 56 runs after anodal stimulation, 20 runs during cathodal stimulation, and 20 runs after cathodal stimulation (see Table 1 for details of the number of runs acquired per monkey).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data.

claim: A total of 136 runs were acquired under anesthesia.
source: A total of 136 runs were acquired under anesthesia: 40 runs before stimulation, 24 runs during 1 mA anodal stimulation, 24 runs after 1 mA anodal stimulation, 24 runs during 2 mA anodal stimulation, and 24 runs after 2 mA anodal stimulation (see Table 1 for details of the number of runs acquired per monkey).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data.

claim: Anesthesia was induced with an intramuscular injection of ketamine (10 mg/kg, Virbac, France) and dexmedetomidine (20 μg/kg, Ovion Pharma, USA).
source: Anesthesia was induced with an intramuscular injection of ketamine (10 mg/kg, Virbac, France) and dexmedetomidine (20 μg/kg, Ovion Pharma, USA)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Anesthesia was maintained with a target-controlled infusion (TCI) of propofol using the 'Paedfusor' pharmacokinetic model.
source: and maintained with a target-controlled infusion (TCI) (Alaris PK Syringe pump, CareFusion, CA, USA) of propofol (Panpharma Fresenius Kabi, France) using the 'Paedfusor' pharmacokinetic model (Absalom and Kenny, 2005) (Monkey R: TCI 5.8 μg/ml, Monkey N: TCI 4.3 μg/ml).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A muscle-blocking agent (cisatracurium, GlaxoSmithKline, France, 0.15 mg/kg, bolus i.v., followed by a continuous infusion rate of 0.18 mg/kg/hr) was used during all anesthesia fMRI sessions to avoid artifacts.
source: A muscle-blocking agent (cisatracurium, GlaxoSmithKline, France, 0.15 mg/kg, bolus i.v., followed by a continuous infusion rate of 0.18 mg/kg/hr) was used during all anesthesia fMRI sessions to avoid artifacts.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Functional images were reoriented, realigned, resampled (1 mm isotropic), smoothed (Gaussian kernel, 3 mm full width at half maximum), and rigidly co-registered to the anatomical template of the monkey MNI space.
source: Functional images were reoriented, realigned, resampled (1 mm isotropic), smoothed (Gaussian kernel, 3 mm full width at half maximum), and rigidly co-registered to the anatomical template of the monkey MNI space (Frey et al., 2011) using custom-made scripts (Uhrig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The global signal was regressed out from the images to remove any confounding effects due to physiological changes.
source: The global signal was regressed out from the images to remove any confounding effects due to physiological cha-nges (e.g., respiratory or cardiac variations).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Voxel time series were filtered with low-pass (0.05 Hz cutoff) and high-pass (0.0025 Hz cutoff) filters and a zero-phase fast Fourier notch filter (0.03 Hz) to remove an artifactual pure frequency present in all the data.
source: Voxel time series were filtered with low-pass (0.05 Hz cutoff) and high-pass (0.0025 Hz cutoff) filters and a zero-phase fast Fourier notch filter (0.03 Hz) to remove an artifactual pure frequency present in all the data (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Uhrig et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: A total of 295 runs were analyzed in the following conditions: awake state, 190 runs and anesthesia, 105 runs.
source: Finally, a total of 295 runs were analyzed in the following conditions: awake state, 190 runs (before tDCS, 82 runs; during anodal tDCS, 38 runs; after anodal tDCS, 39 runs; during cathodal tDCS, 15 runs; after cathodal tDCS, 16 runs) and anesthesia, 105 runs (before tDCS, 34 runs; during 1 mA anodal tDCS, 18 runs; after 1 mA anodal tDCS, 18 runs; during 2 mM anodal tDCS, 17 runs; after 2 mA anodal tDCS, 18 runs).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis.

claim: Anatomical connectivity data were obtained from a recent macaque connectome generated by coupling diffusion MRI tractography with axonal tract tracing studies.
source: Anatomical connectivity data were obtained from a recent macaque connectome generated by coupling diffusion MRI tractography with axonal tract tracing studies (Bakker et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The macaque cortex was subdivided using the Regional Map parcellation method.
source: The macaque cortex was subdivided using the Regional Map parcellation method (Kötter and Wanke, 2005).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The parcellation includes 82 cortical ROIs (41 ROIs per hemisphere).
source: The parcellation includes 82 cortical ROIs (41 ROIs per hemisphere).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The k-means clustering algorithm was utilized using the L2 'Euclidean' distance metric.
source: Each resulting matrix was subjected to the k-means clustering algorithm utilizing the L2 'Euclidean' distance metric.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The inter-pattern correlation variance (IPCV) was employed as the primary method to determine the most appropriate number of clusters.
source: To determine the most appropriate number of clusters, we employed the IPCV as the primary method, as we are mainly interested in the centroids' aspect, supplemented by the elbow method for confirmation.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: The linear slope coefficient of the relationship between the occurrence rate of each centroid and the corresponding centroid/anatomical correlation was computed.
source: Last, we computed the linear slope coefficient of the relationship between the occurrence rate of each centroid and the corresponding centroid/anatomical correlation (i.e., the SFC) to establish a possible tendency for functional states with higher (or lower) correlation to the anatomy.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: For each condition, the histogram associated with the total time of visits of each pattern was computed.
source: For each condition, we computed the histogram associated with the total time of visits of each pattern.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: A Markov chain was built from the empirical frequencies of transitions between patterns.
source: We reckon the sequence of 'patterns visited' as a sequence of random variables that jumps from one pattern to another pattern with a certain probability given by the empirical frequencies in which these transitioning events happen in the sequence. From these empirical frequencies, we built a Markov chain, as done previously (Demertzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Independent T-tests with Bonferroni correction were performed to assess the statistical significance of comparing different conditions.
source: To assess the statistical significance of comparing different conditions and differences in occurrence rates, slopes' coefficients, and Shannon entropy, we performed independent T-tests with Bonferroni correction between the awake and anesthesia conditions before any stimulation and all their associated stimulation conditions and reported the associated p-values.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

claim: Three- or two-way ANOVA was performed to confirm that the obtained results of comparing two conditions together are consistent with comparing the conditions given the independent variables at play.
source: We also performed three- or two-way ANOVA to confirm that the obtained results of comparing two conditions together (with corrections for multiple comparisons) are consistent with comparing the conditions given the independent variables at play: during/after stimulation, amperage/montage used, and the animal; and to evaluate possible interactions between said variables.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

claim: A bootstrap method was performed to ensure the reliability of the transition probabilities.
source: To ensure the reliability of the transition probabilities, we performed a bootstrap method that breaks the temporal dependencies in the chain of visited states.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

claim: The randomization was performed 10,000 times per condition and as many transition matrices were computed.
source: We performed this randomization 10,000 times per condition and computed as many transition matrices.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis methods.

claim: Brain pattern 6 showed the most numerous and strongest differences in visit frequency in awake animals.
source: Brain pattern 6, referred to as the 'anatomical pattern' due to its highest correlation with the CoCoMac connectome, showed the most numerous and strongest differences in visit frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The time spent in brain pattern 6 increased sharply during and following stimulation with the cathodal montage compared to before stimulation and to the corresponding conditions with the anodal montage.
source: The time spent in this pattern increased sharply during and following stimulation with the cathodal montage compared to before stimulation and to the corresponding conditions with the anodal montage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The time spent in brain state 5 was markedly shorter in the cathodal post-stimulation condition compared to pre-stimulation.
source: The time spent in brain state 5 was markedly shorter in the cathodal post-stimulation condition compared to pre-stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cathodal stimulation shortened the time spent in brain state 3 during stimulation compared to the corresponding condition with the anodal montage.
source: Cathodal stimulation also shortened the time spent in brain state 3 during stimulation compared to the corresponding condition with the anodal montage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The distribution of pattern occupancies during or following stimulation with the anodal montage did not exhibit much change compared to pre-stimulation.
source: In sharp contrast, the distribution of pattern occupancies during or following stimulation with the anodal montage did not exhibit much change compared to pre-stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The cathodal stimulation lowered the occurrence of patterns with high frontal coherence (patterns 1, 3, and 5), but promoted the visit of patterns with predominant parieto-occipital coherence (patterns 2 and 4) or very low coherence (pattern 6).
source: These results suggest that the cathodal stimulation lowered the occurrence of patterns with high frontal coherence (patterns 1, 3, and 5), but promoted the visit of patterns with predominant parieto-occipital coherence (patterns 2 and 4) or very low coherence (pattern 6).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The alterations of brain dynamics by cathodal tDCS were not accompanied by any obvious behavioral changes in the monkeys.
source: It should be noted that these alterations of brain dynamics were not accompanied by any obvious behavioral changes in the monkeys, as they continued to show consistent and optimal eye fixation rates (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Table 2.

claim: The Shannon entropy was considerably lower during and after cathodal stimulation compared to before stimulation and during cathodal stimulation compared to during anodal stimulation.
source: The Shannon entropy was considerably lower during and after cathodal stimulation compared to before stimulation and during cathodal stimulation compared to during anodal stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and statistical analyses in Table 4.

claim: The Shannon entropy was not affected by stimulation with the anodal montage.
source: In contrast, the Shannon entropy was not affected by stimulation with the anodal montage, further supporting the polarity-dependent nature of the effects.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Cathodal, but not anodal stimulation limits the degree of surprise held in the distribution of pattern rates.
source: This result implies that cathodal, but not anodal stimulation limits the degree of surprise held in the distribution of pattern rates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Shannon entropy results.

claim: A lower Shannon entropy was reported in many different studies investigating anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness in humans and in macaques.
source: A lower Shannon entropy was reported in many different studies investigating anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness in humans (Golkowski et al., 2019; Castro et al., 2024b), in macaques (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Uhrig et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A lower Shannon entropy was reported under sleep-induced loss of consciousness in humans.
source: A lower Shannon entropy was reported in many different studies investigating anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness in humans (Golkowski et al., 2019; Castro et al., 2024b), in macaques (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Uhrig et al., 2018), under sleep-induced loss of consciousness in humans (Patel et al., 2020; Castro et al., 2024b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A lower Shannon entropy was reported in patients suffering from DOCs.
source: A lower Shannon entropy was reported in many different studies investigating anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness in humans (Golkowski et al., 2019; Castro et al., 2024b), in macaques (Barttfeld et al., 2015; Uhrig et al., 2018), under sleep-induced loss of consciousness in humans (Patel et al., 2020; Castro et al., 2024b), and in patients suffering from DOCs (Demertzi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recovery from general anesthesia in humans was associated with recovery of a higher Shannon entropy value.
source: Moreover, recovery from general anesthesia in humans (Patel et al., 2020; Castro et al., 2024b) and restoration of arousal and wakefulness in anesthetized macaques by deep brain stimulation of the central thalamus (Tasserie et al., 2022; Luppi et al., 2024) were both associated with recovery of a higher Shannon entropy value.
